metadata.title: The Internal State of an LLM Knows When It's Lying

problem.statement: Large Language Models (LLMs) frequently generate inaccurate or false information with a confident tone, which can cause significant harm as users may accept the LLM as a knowledgeable source.
limitations_of_prior_work: LLMs tend to hallucinate facts and provide inaccurate information using confident and compelling language (Ji et al., 2023).

Existing methods for reducing hallucination often assume the LLM is a black box or require fine-tuning, which may cause a model to not perform as well on other tasks (Peng et al., 2023; Bakker et al., 2022; Ouyang et al., 2022; Kirkpatrick et al., 2017).

Contrast-Consistent Search (CCS) requires rephrasing a statement into a question, evaluating the LLM on two different versions of the prompt, and requires training data from the same dataset (topic) as the test set (Burns et al., 2022).
Most prior works on hallucination consider it in relation to a given input (e.g., a passage) that the model operates on, rather than the veracity of the LLM's output without a specific input.

method.name: Statement Accuracy Prediction, based on Language Model Activations (SAPLMA)
method.key_idea: SAPLMA trains a classifier to output the probability that a statement is truthful, based on the hidden layer activations of an LLM as it reads or generates the statement.

components.name: LLM (Facebook OPT-6.7b, LLAMA2-7b)
components.function: Generates or reads statements, providing hidden layer activations from its 32 layers.

components.name: Classifier
components.function: Receives as input the activation values from selected hidden layers of the LLM and determines if a statement is true or false.

techniques.name: Feedforward neural network
techniques.purpose: Serve as the classifier for SAPLMA.
techniques.details: Features three hidden layers with decreasing numbers of hidden units (256, 128, 64), all utilizing ReLU activations, and a final sigmoid output layer.

techniques.name: Adam optimizer
techniques.details: The classifier is trained for 5 epochs.

techniques.name: Out-of-distribution training
techniques.purpose: Ensure the classifier extracts the LLM's internal belief about truthfulness generally, rather than learning topic-specific patterns.
techniques.details: For each topic in the true-false dataset, the classifier is trained using activation values obtained from all other topics and tested on the current topic.

methodology.architecture: The base LLMs are Facebook OPT-6.7b and LLAMA2-7b, both composed of 32 layers. The SAPLMA classifier is a relatively shallow feedforward neural network.
methodology.training_objective: Binary classification to predict whether a statement is true or false based on the LLM's hidden layer values.
methodology.training_data: A custom 'true-false dataset' comprising 6,084 sentences from 6 different topics ('Cities', 'Inventions', 'Chemical Elements', 'Animals', 'Companies', and 'Scientific Facts').
methodology.inference_cost: Requires very little computational power at inference time and can be computed alongside the LLM’s output.

datasets.name: true-false dataset
datasets.size: 6,084 sentences (1,458 Cities, 876 Inventions, 930 Chemical Elements, 1,008 Animals, 1,200 Companies, 612 Scientific Facts)

settings: Out-of-distribution training for SAPLMA on the true-false dataset (trained on all topics except the test topic).
SAPLMA trained on the entire true-false dataset and tested on LLM-generated sentences.
Few-shot baselines provided with truth values from the same topic as the test set.
LLM-generated sentences created using the most probable next word at each step (no sampling).
Optimal threshold for classification determined from a held-out validation set (30% of the generated sentences) for Table 4 results.

main_findings.claim: SAPLMA (20th-layer, OPT-6.7b) achieves significantly higher average accuracy in classifying truthfulness of externally generated sentences compared to baselines.
SAPLMA (16th-layer, LLAMA2-7b) achieves the highest average accuracy in classifying truthfulness of externally generated sentences.
main_findings.comparison: vs. other SAPLMA layer configurations (e.g., last-layer 0.7107, 28th-layer 0.7321, 24th-layer 0.7622, 20th-layer 0.8060)

main_findings.claim: SAPLMA (28th-layer, OPT-6.7b) outperforms baselines in classifying truthfulness of sentences generated by the LLM itself, using a 0.5 threshold.
SAPLMA (28th-layer, OPT-6.7b) accuracy improves on LLM-generated sentences when using an optimal threshold from a validation set.
GPT-4 achieves high accuracy when prompted to determine the truthfulness of LLM-generated statements.
main_findings.setting: prompting with 30 statements at a time

ablation_insights.component: Randomly permuted true/false labels in training data
ablation_insights.effect: The average accuracy on the random training data is significantly lower, indicating the model exploits data structure.
ablation_insights.delta: Drops from 86.4% (average training accuracy for SAPLMA with OPT-6.7b’s 20th layer) to 62.5%.

contributions.description: The release of a dataset of true-false statements along with a method for generating such information.
Demonstrating that an LLM might “know” when a statement that it has just generated is false, and proposing SAPLMA, a method for extracting this information.

comparisons.difference: SAPLMA leverages LLM hidden layer activations, while BERT uses its own embeddings.
comparisons.evidence: SAPLMA (0.7098 average accuracy) outperforms BERT (0.5434 average accuracy) on externally generated sentences using OPT-6.7b.

comparisons.difference: SAPLMA uses a separate classifier trained on hidden states, whereas few-shot learning directly prompts the LLM.
comparisons.evidence: SAPLMA (0.7098 average accuracy) outperforms 3-shot (0.5374) and 5-shot (0.5370) on externally generated sentences using OPT-6.7b.

comparisons.difference: LLM-assigned sentence probability is highly susceptible to syntax, exact words, and statement length, making it a weak signal for veracity, while SAPLMA's internal state analysis is more reliable.
comparisons.evidence: SAPLMA (0.7098 average accuracy) outperforms the It-is-true baseline (0.5593 average accuracy) on externally generated sentences using OPT-6.7b.

comparisons.difference: CCS requires specific prompt rephrasing and training data from the same topic as the test set, making it unsuitable for general LLM-generated statements, unlike SAPLMA.
comparisons.evidence: CCS increases accuracy by only approximately 4% over the 0-shot LLM query, while our approach demonstrates a nearly 20% increase over the 0-shot LLM.

limitations: The paper primarily focuses on detecting if a statement is true or false, but in practice, it may be more beneficial to detect if the LLM is positive about a statement's correctness or if it is unsure.
The work was only tested in English.

The activation values were collected when each sentence was generated separately; in longer responses, activation values develop over time and would need to be decoupled to test the most recent statement's truthfulness.
Certain ethical issues, such as bias, may persist and potentially be transferred from the LLM to SAPLMA.
future_work: Apply the method to larger LLMs.
Run experiments with humans to demonstrate increased trust and understanding of LLM limitations when augmented with SAPLMA.
Study how the activations develop over time as additional words are generated.
Consider fusing multiple layers together and using intermediate activation values for all words in a statement.
Consider providing SAPLMA with the probabilities of the generated words.
Adapt the approach to bias mitigation.

key_terms.definition: Generating inaccurate or false information with a confident tone.

key_terms.term: Statement Accuracy Prediction, based on Language Model Activations (SAPLMA)
key_terms.definition: A method designed to determine the truthfulness of statements generated by an LLM using the values in its hidden layers.
A fact that is universally acknowledged without needing to be explicitly stated.
